draft.title: Sampling methods
card: every member of the population, the whole group being studied, has an equal chance of being in the sample, such as drawing names from a hat.
choose every kth member from a list, after a random start. For 500 students and a sample of 50, take every 10th name.
split the population into groups, such as year groups, then take a random sample from each group in proportion to its size.
people choose to take part, such as in an online poll. People with strong views are more likely to reply, so the sample can be biased: its results may not match the population.
draft.remember: A fair sample gives every member an equal chance of being chosen. A sample whose members choose themselves can be biased.

a.q: A school keeps a numbered list of its 500 students. The principal picks a random start, then surveys every 10th student on the list. Which sampling method is this?
a.why: Choosing every kth name from a list after a random start is systematic sampling. It is not stratified, because the students are not split into groups first.
a.clue: Look at how the students are picked from the list.

b.q: The council in Toowoomba wants to know if residents like a new bus timetable. It posts a survey link on its Facebook page and uses the first 200 replies. Why might the results be biased?
opts: Residents chose to reply, so they may not match the town
Residents were split into groups, so some may be left out
Every resident had an equal chance, so some may be missed
Every 10th reply was used, so some groups may be skipped
b.why: This is a self-selected sample. Only residents who see the page and choose to reply take part, so their views may not match the whole town. The council did not split residents into groups or take every 10th reply, and not every resident had an equal chance of being chosen.
b.clue: Who decided which residents took part?

b.best: Residents chose to reply, so they may not match the town
